course.title: Audit Solana Programs: Exploit, Harden, Fuzz
course.one_line_promise: By the end you can take an unfamiliar Solana program, find the planted vulnerabilities, ship the fixes, and prove it with a fuzz harness — the way an auditor does.

prerequisites: has shipped a PDA + CPI program
comfortable reading Rust and running anchor test

glossary.def: Verifying an account is owned by the expected program before trusting its data.

brief.title: Break it before you defend it

objectives.statement: find and trigger a planted vulnerability in a small Solana program

brief.hook: You've shipped programs that 'worked.' Here's one that works too — and drains its vault in one transaction. Your job today isn't to fix it. It's to break it.
brief.concept_spec: The auditor's mindset: assume every account and input is hostile. Worked example: an unguarded withdraw that anyone can call. One new element: reading a program adversarially.
brief.artifact_spec: A vulnerable counter-vault program; the learner writes a test that drains it.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: finish the exploit test that calls withdraw as the wrong signer (TODO). Solo: find a second way to break it. Accept: the exploit test passes (the program is drained).
brief.the_tradeoff: Exploit-first teaches the why fast, BUT it's only safe on intentionally vulnerable code — never run these moves on programs you don't own.

footguns: assuming the happy path is the only path
trusting an account because it has the right shape

brief.assessment: the learner's exploit test drains the vulnerable program
brief.voice_notes: security: be wary of Hotz reductive collapse — exploits are concrete, don't over-simplify the fix. Helius expository craft.

brief.title: Signer and owner checks: the cheap fixes that matter most

objectives.statement: add signer and owner checks that close an authorization hole

brief.hook: The drain you just wrote worked because the program never checked who was calling or who owned the account. Two lines would have stopped it. Let's add them — and see them block your exploit.
brief.concept_spec: Signer checks (is_signer) and owner checks (account.owner == expected program). Build it twice: the native check, then the Anchor constraint that generates it. One new element: the owner check.
brief.artifact_spec: Harden the vault: require the authority to sign and validate account ownership; re-run the exploit and watch it fail.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: add the missing has_one / signer constraint (TODO). Solo: add an owner check on a second account. Accept: the previous exploit test now fails; the legitimate path passes.
brief.the_tradeoff: Anchor constraints make these checks declarative and hard to forget, BUT they hide what's enforced — knowing the native check is what lets you audit code that doesn't use them.

footguns: trusting Anchor to add a check you never declared

brief.assessment: anchor test: the exploit now reverts; the authorized path still works
brief.voice_notes: build-it-twice guest: native check then Anchor constraint; the 'two lines' callback to the exploit is the seam.

brief.title: Canonical bumps and seed hygiene

objectives.statement: explain why a non-canonical bump is a forgery and why seed schemes must be validated
store and check the canonical bump and validate seeds

brief.hook: Your PDA derivation 'worked' in testing. But an attacker can pass a different valid bump, or craft seeds that collide with another user's account. Why does Solana even allow that?
brief.concept_spec: Canonical vs non-canonical bumps; storing the bump; validating user-influenced seeds. Derive WHY find_program_address returns the canonical bump and why accepting any bump is exploitable. One new element: bump canonicalization.
brief.artifact_spec: Harden the vault's PDA: store the canonical bump on init, check it on use, and reject crafted seeds.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: replace the accepted-bump arg with the stored canonical bump (TODO). Solo: write a test that tries a non-canonical bump and must fail. Accept: forged-bump and colliding-seed attempts revert.
brief.the_tradeoff: Storing the bump costs a byte and a check, BUT recomputing or trusting a passed-in bump is both slower and a security hole — the canonical bump is the only safe one.

footguns: accepting a bump as an instruction arg

brief.assessment: anchor test: forged-bump and colliding-seed attacks revert; legitimate access works
brief.voice_notes: contested/intricate design → Vitalik craft over spine; derive why canonical bump is the only safe one.

brief.title: Overflow and the programs you call

objectives.statement: replace unchecked arithmetic with checked operations
validate a CPI target program id to prevent arbitrary CPI

brief.hook: A u64 that wraps from zero to four billion, and a 'token program' the caller gets to choose. Two of the nastiest Solana exploits hide in plain arithmetic and one unchecked address.
brief.concept_spec: Checked arithmetic (checked_add/sub/mul) vs silent overflow; arbitrary-CPI (validating the program id you invoke). One new element per beat: overflow, then CPI target validation.
brief.artifact_spec: Harden the vault: make all balance math checked, and validate the token program id before the deposit CPI.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: swap the + for checked_add returning an error (TODO). Solo: add a program-id check before the CPI. Accept: an overflow test reverts; a swapped-program CPI reverts.
brief.the_tradeoff: Checked math and program-id validation add a few lines and a few compute units, BUT skipping them is how vaults get drained — correctness beats the micro-optimization here.

footguns: trusting a token account's mint without checking

brief.assessment: anchor test: overflow path reverts; a substituted CPI program reverts
brief.voice_notes: documented mechanisms → Helius expository; two clean beats, one new element each.

brief.title: Find the bug you didn't think of: fuzzing

objectives.statement: write a fuzz test that asserts a program invariant and catches a regression

brief.hook: Your tests pass — but they only check the cases you imagined. Fuzzing throws millions of cases you didn't. Let's point one at your vault and see what it finds.
brief.concept_spec: Property/invariant fuzzing for Solana programs with Trident; expressing an invariant (e.g. total deposited never exceeds vault balance). One new element: the fuzz harness as a thread on top of the existing tests.
brief.artifact_spec: Add a Trident fuzz target asserting a balance invariant on the hardened vault; reintroduce a bug and watch the fuzzer catch it.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: fill in the invariant assertion (TODO). Solo: add a second invariant. Accept: the fuzzer flags a deliberately reintroduced overflow.
brief.the_tradeoff: Fuzzing surfaces unknown-unknowns, BUT it costs setup and CI time and only checks the invariants you write — it complements, never replaces, targeted tests and review.

footguns: asserting no invariants (a fuzzer with nothing to check finds nothing)

brief.assessment: the fuzz target catches a reintroduced bug; the clean program passes
brief.voice_notes: testing-thread escalation; cite the Trident tool name as grounded in research.

claims.evidence: TODO: confirm before writing the lab

open_questions: Teach Trident, or the newer anchor-native fuzzing path? Confirm via the kit before the lab.
frozen_facts: Fuzzing asserts invariants over many generated inputs; it complements, never replaces, targeted tests.
A fuzzer only finds violations of the invariants you actually assert.

brief.title: Audit an unfamiliar program (the CTF)

objectives.statement: audit an unfamiliar program: find the planted bugs, ship fixes, and add a fuzz test

brief.hook: Here's a program you've never seen, with several planted vulnerabilities. Find them, fix them, and prove it — exactly like a real engagement.
brief.concept_spec: Integration: apply the full checklist (signer/owner, PDA/bump, arithmetic, CPI) to unfamiliar code, then back the fixes with a fuzz test. No new primitive — this is the consolidation.
brief.artifact_spec: An unfamiliar vulnerable program; the learner produces a findings list, a fixed version, and a fuzz test that catches a regression.
brief.exercise_spec: Solo: audit, fix, and fuzz. Accept: all planted bugs identified and fixed; the fuzz test catches a reintroduced bug; legitimate paths pass.
brief.the_tradeoff: A timed CTF rewards pattern-matching speed, BUT real audits also need the patience to read the boring code — the planted bugs hide where attention drops.

footguns: fixing a symptom instead of the missing check

brief.assessment: all planted vulns found + fixed; a fuzz test catches a regression; findings written up
brief.voice_notes: course close; spine carries it; celebrate the auditor's eye, name the trade-off of speed vs patience.

assessment.gate_principle: Completion is gated on finding, fixing, and fuzzing real bugs — never on watching.
